newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia takes aims at APEC's aviation rules.
newsitem.headline: Australia takes aims at APEC's aviation rules.

text.p: Australia plans to persuade APEC to free up regional regulation on air freight and raise the profile of aviation safety, Transport Minister John Sharp said on Friday.
"The government will be taking forward to APEC in the coming year proposals to free up the regional regulation of air freight," he said.
Sharp said he would raise the issue when transport ministers of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum meet in Canada in June 1997.
"Australia sees a role for APEC in raising the profile within governments of competitive air services, technical regulation and its impact on safety and trade in the APEC programme," he said.
APEC needs to develop an air freight policy agreement that would provide greater opportunities for third country freight operators on outbound routes, Sharp said.
He said Australia had substantially liberalised its international air freight market in order for Australian exporters to tap growing demand for time-sensitive goods such as fresh food products.

"I do believe it is in the interests of all trading nations in the region to reduce the barriers to the development of dedicated air freight capacity that exist with the current arrangements," said Sharp, who is a pilot.

APEC groups Australia, Brunei, Canada, Chile, China, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Mexico, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, the Philippines, Singapore, Taiwan, Thailand and the United States.
The minister also unveiled plans for new passenger air services linking sparsely populated northern Australia to its neighbours in the Asia-Pacific region.
"Australia is pursuing the development of regional airlinks between north Australia and other countries to its near north," Sharp said.

He said the plan would link Darwin in the Northern Territory with regional centres in Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Brunei and Papua New Guinea. It would exclude the major cities in each country such as Sydney, Manila, Jakarta and Kuala Lumpur.
Sharp said the goal was "to build regional links that are attractive to airlines, niche operators and or tourism investors."
